Every number is the average, and equal does not count, so the answer is 0.
The average is 22.0, so only the 100 beats it. One big item pulls the average above most of the list.
The average is 30.0, and 30 itself does not count, so only 40 and 50 do.

questions.fb: Some jobs need two passes over the same list: one to work the average out, one to compare against it.

questions.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.

teach.say: A list, a loop and an if together: the loop visits every item and the if decides what happens to it.

questions.fb: Two items are bigger than 5, and 5 itself is not one of them. len() still counts every item, whatever the if decided.

questions.q: Change the program so it counts the numbers that are `5` or more instead of the numbers that are more than `5`.
brief: Change only the comparison.
Exactly `5` now counts.
Display exactly: 3

hint.think: Which comparison lets the two sides be equal?

tests.why: A 2 means the comparison still leaves the 5 out. >= allows the two sides to be equal.

questions.fb: One character decides whether the boundary value counts, and that is the commonest place for a counting program to go wrong.

questions.q: Finish the program so it displays only the words longer than three letters, one on each line.
brief: Replace ____ with the comparison.
A word of exactly three letters is not longer than three.
Three lines of output: `"fern"`, then `"rose"`, then `"holly"`.

hint.think: len() of the word counts its letters, and that count has to be compared with `3`.

tests.why: ivy and oak have three letters each, so > 3 leaves them out while >= 3 would let them in.

questions.fb: An if inside a loop lets some items through and not others, and len() is what turns a word into a number to test.

questions.q: This program should display the total of the five numbers typed in. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and read the error message.
The user types in five lines, one whole number on each.
One line of output, which is one number.

hint.think: What does input() always hand back, whatever the user typed?

questions.starter:
nums = []
for i in range(5):
    nums.append(input())
total = 0
for n in nums:
    total = total + n
print(total)

tests.why: A TypeError here means the list is holding text. Cast each line with int() as it is read.
Casting belongs on the way in, as the value is read, not after the total has been built.
int() handles a negative number just as well, so the total is allowed to go down.

questions.fb: A list is only as good as what went into it. input() hands back text every time, so cast it as it arrives.

questions.q: Ask the user for six whole numbers, one on each line. Keep them in one list. Add them all up. Work out their average, rounded to `1` decimal place. Display the total. Then display the average on the next line.
brief: The user types in six lines, one whole number on each.
Line 1 is the total, which is a whole number.
Line 2 is the average, rounded to `1` decimal place.
Dividing always gives a decimal, so an average of 12 is displayed as 12.0.

hint.think: The total is built inside the loop, and the average is worked out from it afterwards.

questions.starter: # Six numbers in, the total and then the average out

tests.why: The total is displayed as a whole number and the average rounded to one decimal place.
Every item the same still needs both lines, and dividing gives a decimal, so 11.0 and not 11.
A long run of decimals on line 2 means the round() is missing.
All zeros give a total of 0 and an average of 0.0, and both lines still have to be displayed.

questions.fb: The total grows inside the loop, and the average comes from the finished total and the length of the list.

questions.q: Ask the user for five words, one on each line. Keep them in one list. Then ask for a word to look for. Count how many times that word is in the list. Display that count.
brief: The user types in six lines: five words, then the word to look for.
Count every match, not only the first one.
One line of output, which is one number.
Display `0` when the word is not in the list at all.

hint.think: Go through the list and compare each item with the word being looked for.
start: # then a loop over the list with an if inside it

questions.starter: # Five words in, then how many times one of them appears

tests.why: Three of the five words are ivy, so the counter goes up three times.
Nothing matches, so the counter stays at 0, and that 0 still has to be displayed.
All five items match. A 1 means the loop stopped at the first match instead of carrying on.
Only the last item matches, so a loop that stopped before the end would miss it.

questions.fb: Counting matches is the same counter and if as counting large numbers: only the comparison changes.

questions.q: Ask the user for seven whole numbers, one on each line. Keep them in one list. Find the largest one with a loop of your own. Work out which position it sits at, counting from `0`. Display the largest. Then display its position on the next line.
brief: The user types in seven lines, one whole number on each.
Some of the numbers may be negative.
When two items are equally large, the earlier position wins.
Do not use max() or .index().

hint.think: Count through the positions, so the position of the best one can be remembered as well as the value.
walk: Go through the positions of the list.
Replace the best position only when the item there is strictly larger.
Display the item at the best position, then the position itself.

questions.starter: # Seven numbers in, the largest and where it sits
forbid: Find the largest with a loop of your own rather than using max().
Work the position out as you go rather than looking it up with .index().

tests.why: The largest is the third item, which is position 2 - a 3 means the counting started at 1.
With every item equal the first one is the largest, so the position is 0.
Two items are 20 and the earlier one wins, so compare with > and not >= when you replace the best position.
All seven are negative, so a best that started at 0 would wrongly say 0. Start it at the first item.
The largest is the very last item, position 6, so a loop that stops one short never sees it.

questions.fb: Remembering the position instead of the value gives you both, because the value is always nums[best].
